entries.lesson_core_move: Model the RC low-pass circuit by identifying the series resistor, shunt capacitor, and capacitor-voltage output as the physical LTI filter used for later differential-equation and frequency-response analysis.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Series Resistor and Shunt Capacitor

image_slots.image_description: A clean schematic of the standard RC low-pass circuit with $v_{in}(t)$ entering a series resistor $R$, a shunt capacitor $C$ to ground, and the output node after the resistor. Keep the drawing uncluttered and pedagogical, emphasize topology over numerical values, and make the output node obvious.

The same standard RC low-pass topology mirrored left-to-right, with the source and output node swapped visually but the resistor still in the signal path and the capacitor still shunting to ground. Keep labels minimal so the learner identifies roles from the wiring, not the layout.

prompt_blocks.text: In the standard RC low-pass circuit shown, which choice correctly identifies the series resistor and the shunt capacitor?
Choose the option that matches the resistor on the signal path and the capacitor that goes to ground.

choice_blocks.text: The resistor on the signal path is the series resistor, and the capacitor from the output node to ground is the shunt capacitor.
The capacitor from the output node to ground is the series resistor, and the resistor on the signal path is the shunt capacitor.
The source labeled $v_{in}(t)$ is the series resistor, and the output node is the shunt capacitor.
The resistor on the signal path is the shunt capacitor, and the capacitor from the output node to ground is the series resistor.
The branch from the output node to ground is the series path, and the resistor on that path is the shunt element.

questions.correct_answer: The resistor on the signal path is the series resistor, and the capacitor from the output node to ground is the shunt capacitor.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Trace the input path from $v_{in}(t)$ to the first component: that resistor is in series. The capacitor branch that leaves the output node and goes to ground is the shunt capacitor.

prompt_blocks.text: In the mirrored RC low-pass circuit shown below, which choice still correctly identifies the series resistor and the shunt capacitor?
The layout is flipped, but the topology is the same. Choose the option that still follows the signal path and the branch to ground.

choice_blocks.text: The resistor in the signal path is the series resistor, and the capacitor branch to ground is the shunt capacitor.
The capacitor branch to ground is the series resistor, and the resistor in the signal path is the shunt capacitor.
The source arrow is the series resistor, and the output node is the shunt capacitor.
The capacitor in the signal path is the series resistor, and the resistor branch to ground is the shunt capacitor.
The output node is the series resistor, and the source arrow is the shunt capacitor.

questions.correct_answer: The resistor in the signal path is the series resistor, and the capacitor branch to ground is the shunt capacitor.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Flipping the drawing does not change the circuit roles. The element on the signal path is still the series resistor, and the branch from the output node to ground is still the shunt capacitor.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Capacitor Voltage as the Output Signal

image_slots.image_description: A clean RC low-pass schematic with $v_{in}(t)$ entering a series resistor $R$, a shunt capacitor $C$ to ground, an explicit output arrow across the capacitor, and visible node labels $v_C(t)$ and $v_R(t)$. Keep the circuit uncluttered and make the capacitor branch and output marker obvious.

The same RC low-pass schematic with $v_{in}(t)$ entering a series resistor $R$ and a shunt capacitor $C$ to ground, with visible node labels $v_C(t)$ and $v_R(t)$ but no explicit output arrow. Keep the capacitor branch visually prominent so the learner must infer that the output is the capacitor voltage.

prompt_blocks.text: Look at the RC low-pass schematic.
Which labeled voltage is the output signal across the capacitor?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The output is measured across the capacitor, so the correct signal is the capacitor voltage.
$v_{in}(t)$ is the input, $v_R(t)$ is the resistor voltage, and $i(t)$ or $q(t)$ are not output voltages.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the same RC low-pass circuit, but focus on the signal across the capacitor branch.
Which signal should be treated as the output?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The filter output is the voltage across the capacitor branch, so it is $v_C(t)$.
$v_{in}(t)$ stays the input, $v_R(t)$ stays the resistor voltage, and $i(t)$ is not the output voltage.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the RC Low-Pass Circuit as an Input-Output Filter

image_slots.image_description: A clean schematic of the standard RC low-pass circuit annotated with an input arrow at the source, a series resistor $R$, a shunt capacitor $C$ to ground, and an output arrow across the capacitor. Emphasize signal flow from source to capacitor, keep the diagram uncluttered, and make the system boundary obvious.

A clean schematic of the same RC low-pass circuit with $v_{in}(t)$ marked at the source, $v_R(t)$ labeled across the resistor, and $v_{out}(t)=v_C(t)$ labeled across the capacitor. Emphasize the input-output roles and keep the resistor voltage visible as a distractor.

prompt_blocks.text: In the RC low-pass circuit shown, which statement correctly identifies the input and output signals?
Choose the interpretation that matches the system boundary.

choice_blocks.text: The input is $v_{in}(t)$, the output is $v_C(t)$, and the RC network is a driven LTI filter.
The input is $v_C(t)$, the output is $v_{in}(t)$, and the RC network is a driven LTI filter.
The input is $v_{in}(t)$, the output is $v_R(t)$, and the RC network is a driven LTI filter.
The input is $v_{in}(t)$, the output is the capacitor itself, and the RC network is source-free.
The input is $v_R(t)$, the output is $v_C(t)$, and the RC network is a driven LTI filter.

questions.correct_answer: The input is $v_{in}(t)$, the output is $v_C(t)$, and the RC network is a driven LTI filter.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The source-side signal is the input, so it is $v_{in}(t)$. The output is the voltage across the capacitor, so it is $v_C(t)$.
That makes the RC network a driven LTI filter mapping $v_{in}(t)$ to $v_C(t)$, which is the system boundary used later in the lesson.

prompt_blocks.text: In the same RC low-pass circuit, which statement best describes the whole RC network as a system?
Choose the option that treats the circuit as an input-output filter.

choice_blocks.text: It is a driven LTI filter that maps $v_{in}(t)$ to $v_{out}(t)=v_C(t)$.
It is a source-free element with no input signal.
It is a driven LTI filter whose output is $v_R(t)$.
It is a capacitor-only system that outputs the capacitor itself.
It is a feedback loop in which the output feeds back to the source.

questions.correct_answer: It is a driven LTI filter that maps $v_{in}(t)$ to $v_{out}(t)=v_C(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The circuit is driven by $v_{in}(t)$ and produces $v_{out}(t)=v_C(t)$, so it is not source-free. The resistor and capacitor together form the filter between those two signals.
That is the input-output interpretation the later analysis steps reuse.

entries.lesson_core_move: Derive the low-pass input-output differential equation from the RC circuit model by relating resistor current, capacitor current, input voltage, and output voltage.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Low-Pass Input and Capacitor-Voltage Output

prompt_blocks.text: A series resistor feeds a shunt capacitor to ground. The source is labeled $u(t)$ and the capacitor voltage is labeled $v_C(t)$. Which choice correctly identifies the input and the output?

choice_blocks.text: Input the node after the resistor, output $v_C(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The source-side label is the input signal, and the voltage across the capacitor is the output signal.
So the correct pair is input $u(t)$, output $v_C(t)$. The resistor voltage and capacitor current are internal quantities, not the system input-output pair.

prompt_blocks.text: Using the same RC low-pass convention, the source is labeled $v_{in}(t)$ and the capacitor voltage is labeled $v_{out}(t)$. Which choice correctly identifies the input and the output?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The source-side signal is still the input, and the signal across the capacitor is still the output.
So the correct pair is input $v_{in}(t)$, output $v_{out}(t)$. Swapping the roles or replacing the output with $v_R(t)$ or $i_C(t)$ would change the system definition.

sections.section_title: Writing the Resistor Current from the Input-Output Voltage Difference

prompt_blocks.text: For the RC low-pass circuit with input $u(t)$ and output $v_C(t)$, what is the resistor current $i_R(t)$ if the current is defined from the input node to the capacitor node?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The voltage across the resistor is the input-node voltage minus the capacitor-node voltage, so Ohm's law gives current equal to that drop divided by $R$.

prompt_blocks.text: In the same RC low-pass circuit, the source voltage is $v_{in}(t)$ and the capacitor-node voltage is $v_o(t)$. Which expression gives the resistor current from the source node toward the capacitor node?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The resistor current is the input-node voltage minus the capacitor-node voltage, divided by $R$. Renaming the nodes does not change the rule.

sections.section_title: Writing the Capacitor Current from the Output-Voltage Derivative

prompt_blocks.text: For the same RC low-pass circuit, the capacitor voltage is $v_C(t)$. Which expression gives the capacitor current $i_C(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For a capacitor, current equals capacitance times the time derivative of the voltage across it. Since the capacitor voltage here is $v_C(t)$, the current is $i_C(t)=C\frac{dv_C(t)}{dt}$.
The other choices either invert $C$, replace the derivative with the voltage itself, use the input derivative, or flip the sign.

prompt_blocks.text: If the capacitor voltage is $y(t)$ and the capacitance is $3$, which expression gives the capacitor current $i_C(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the capacitor law and substitute the given capacitance: $i_C(t)=C\frac{dy(t)}{dt}$. With $C=3$, this becomes $i_C(t)=3\frac{dy(t)}{dt}$.
The other choices either invert the capacitance, use the voltage itself, use the input derivative, or reverse the sign.

sections.section_title: Equating the Resistor and Capacitor Currents

prompt_blocks.text: Given $i_R(t)=\frac{x(t)-y(t)}{R}$ and $i_C(t)=C\frac{dy(t)}{dt}$, which equation follows from the series-branch connection?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: In a series branch, the same current flows through both elements, so the step is to set $i_R(t)=i_C(t)$ rather than add them.
That equality is the raw low-pass differential-equation step. The next step will only rearrange it.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $i_R(t)=\frac{u(t)-v(t)}{R}$ and $i_C(t)=2C\frac{dv(t)}{dt}$, what equation follows from equating the resistor and capacitor currents?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The label change does not change the rule: the resistor and capacitor are still in series, so the branch current is the same through both elements.
The factor $2$ stays attached to the capacitor current, but the move is unchanged: equate the two currents and keep the branch-direction sign convention.

sections.section_title: Rewriting the Low-Pass Differential Equation in Standard First-Order Form

prompt_blocks.text: Starting from $\frac{x(t)-y(t)}{R}=C\frac{dy(t)}{dt}$, which equation is the standard first-order low-pass form after clearing the denominator and rearranging?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply both sides by $R$ to clear the denominator, then move the $y(t)$ term to the left. That gives the standard first-order form with the derivative term multiplied by $RC$.

prompt_blocks.text: Starting from $\frac{x(t)-y(t)}{R}=C\frac{dy(t)}{dt}$, which equation do you get after dividing through by $RC$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Divide the rearranged equation through by $RC$ so the derivative term has coefficient $1$. The output and input terms each pick up the same factor $\frac{1}{RC}$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert the low-pass differential equation into the frequency response \(H(j\omega)\) that maps sinusoidal input frequency to output amplitude scaling and phase shift.

sections.section_title: Replacing Low-Pass Derivatives with \(j\omega\) Factors

prompt_blocks.text: Starting from $2RC\,\frac{dy(t)}{dt}+y(t)=x(t)$ with $x(t)=Xe^{j\omega t}$ and $y(t)=Ye^{j\omega t}$, replace the derivative with a $j\omega$ factor and write the resulting algebraic equation linking $X$ and $Y$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Replace $\frac{d}{dt}$ on the sinusoidal trial with multiplication by $j\omega$. Because the coefficient on the derivative is $2RC$, the transformed equation becomes $(1+2j\omega RC)Y=X$ after canceling the common exponential.

prompt_blocks.text: Starting from $RC\,\frac{dy(t)}{dt}+y(t)=x(t)$ with $x(t)=Ae^{j\omega t}$ and $y(t)=Be^{j\omega t}$, replace the derivative with a $j\omega$ factor and write the resulting algebraic equation linking $A$ and $B$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The amplitude symbols change from $X$ and $Y$ to $A$ and $B$, but the derivative rule does not change. Substitute the trial forms, replace $\frac{d}{dt}$ with $j\omega$, and cancel the common exponential to get $(1+j\omega RC)B=A$.

sections.section_title: Solving for the Low-Pass Frequency Response

prompt_blocks.text: If $(2+j\omega RC)Y=X$, what is $H(j\omega)=Y/X$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Divide by $X$ to expose the ratio $Y/X$, then divide by $2+j\omega RC$ to isolate $H(j\omega)$. The result is $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2+j\omega RC}$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $X=(3+j\omega RC)Y$, what is $H(j\omega)=Y/X$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Rewriting the equation with the factor on the right does not change the algebra. Divide by $X$ to expose $Y/X$, then divide by $3+j\omega RC$ to isolate $H(j\omega)$. The result is $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{3+j\omega RC}$.

sections.section_title: Evaluating \(H(j\omega)\) at a Specific Frequency

prompt_blocks.text: If $H(j\omega)=1/(1+j\omega RC)$, what is $H(j\omega)$ at $\omega=1/(2RC)$? Simplify your answer to rectangular form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $\omega=1/(2RC)$ into the known response. The move here is evaluation first, then simplification.
Now rationalize the denominator with the conjugate $1-j/2$ to remove the imaginary term from the bottom.
So the simplified rectangular value is $\frac{4-2j}{5}$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $H(j\omega)=1/(1+j\omega RC)$, what is $H(j\omega)$ at $\omega=2/RC$? Simplify your answer to rectangular form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $\omega=2/RC$ into the frequency response. The only work left is to simplify the resulting complex fraction.
Rationalize with the conjugate $1-2j$ to move the value into rectangular form.
So the simplified rectangular value is $\frac{1-2j}{5}$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Amplitude Scaling and Phase Shift from \(H(j\omega)\)

prompt_blocks.text: If $H(j\omega)=\frac{1-j}{4}$, which statement correctly describes the amplitude scaling and phase shift of a unit-amplitude sinusoid at that frequency?

choice_blocks.text: The sinusoid is scaled by $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$ and lags by $\frac{\pi}{4}$.
The sinusoid is scaled by $\frac{1}{4}$ and lags by $\frac{\pi}{4}$.
The sinusoid is scaled by $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$ and leads by $\frac{\pi}{4}$.
The sinusoid is shifted by $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$ and scaled by $\frac{\pi}{4}$.
The sinusoid is scaled by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and lags by $\frac{\pi}{4}$.

questions.correct_answer: The sinusoid is scaled by $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$ and lags by $\frac{\pi}{4}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Take the magnitude and angle of the complex response. Here $|H(j\omega)|=\sqrt{(1/4)^2+(-1/4)^2}=1/(2\sqrt{2})$, and the negative imaginary part with equal real and imaginary sizes puts the angle in the fourth quadrant.
So the sinusoid keeps the same frequency, its amplitude is reduced to $1/(2\sqrt{2})$, and its phase is delayed by $\pi/4$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $H(j\omega)=\frac{1-\sqrt{3}j}{4}$, which statement correctly describes the amplitude scaling and phase shift of a unit-amplitude sinusoid at that frequency?

choice_blocks.text: The sinusoid is scaled by $\frac{1}{2}$ and lags by $\frac{\pi}{3}$.
The sinusoid is scaled by $\frac{1}{4}$ and lags by $\frac{\pi}{3}$.
The sinusoid is scaled by $\frac{1}{2}$ and leads by $\frac{\pi}{3}$.
The sinusoid is shifted by $\frac{1}{2}$ and scaled by $\frac{\pi}{3}$.
The sinusoid is scaled by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and lags by $\frac{\pi}{4}$.

questions.correct_answer: The sinusoid is scaled by $\frac{1}{2}$ and lags by $\frac{\pi}{3}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Compute the magnitude from the real and imaginary parts. Since $|H(j\omega)|=\sqrt{(1/4)^2+(\sqrt{3}/4)^2}=1/2$, the response halves the sinusoid's amplitude.
The imaginary part is negative, so the phase is negative. That means the output is delayed by $\pi/3$ while staying at the same frequency.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the RC low-pass magnitude response from its frequency response and interpret how it passes low frequencies while attenuating high frequencies.

sections.section_title: Computing |H(j\omega)| from the Low-Pass Frequency Response

prompt_blocks.text: Given $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega\tau}$, what is $|H(j\omega)|$ after simplification?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Take the magnitude of the numerator and denominator separately. The numerator has magnitude $1$, and $\left|1+j\omega\tau\right|=\sqrt{1+(\omega\tau)^2}$.
So the simplified magnitude is a real, nonnegative gain expression.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\,2\omega RC}$, what is $|H(j\omega)|$ after simplification?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The numerator still has magnitude $1$. The denominator magnitude is $\left|1+j\,2\omega RC\right|=\sqrt{1+(2\omega RC)^2}$.
So the frequency scaling only changes the argument inside the square root, not the magnitude rule itself.

sections.section_title: Evaluating Low-Frequency Gain for the RC Low-Pass Filter

prompt_blocks.text: What is $|H(j0)|$ for $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega RC}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $\omega=0$ into $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega RC}$. That gives $H(j0)=\frac{1}{1+j0RC}=1$, so the low-frequency gain is $|H(j0)|=1$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is $\lim_{\omega\to 0}|H(j\omega)|$ for $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega RC}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: As $\omega\to 0$, the term $j\omega RC$ goes to $0$, so the response approaches $\frac{1}{1+0}=1$. The low-frequency gain at DC is therefore $1$.

sections.section_title: Evaluating High-Frequency Gain for the RC Low-Pass Filter

prompt_blocks.text: Using $|H(j\omega)|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\omega RC)^2}}$, evaluate $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}|H(j\omega)|$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: As $\omega\to\infty$, the term $(\omega RC)^2$ makes the denominator grow without bound while the numerator stays $1$, so the gain goes to $0$.
That is the high-frequency attenuation behavior of the RC low-pass filter.

prompt_blocks.text: Using $|H(j\omega)|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\omega \tau)^2}}$, evaluate $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}|H(j\omega)|$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The symbol changed from $RC$ to $\tau$, but the high-frequency behavior is the same: the denominator still grows without bound while the numerator stays $1$.
So the RC low-pass gain still tends to $0$ at high frequency, which means the response attenuates rapid oscillations.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Low-Pass Magnitude Response as Passing and Attenuating Frequencies

prompt_blocks.text: Which statement best describes the RC low-pass magnitude response $|H(j\omega)|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\omega RC)^2}}$?

choice_blocks.text: It passes low frequencies and attenuates high frequencies.
It passes high frequencies and attenuates low frequencies.
It has constant gain for all frequencies.
It is identically zero for all frequencies.
Its gain grows without bound as frequency increases.

questions.correct_answer: It passes low frequencies and attenuates high frequencies.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The magnitude is $1$ at low frequency and falls toward $0$ as $\omega$ increases. That means slowly varying components are passed more strongly, while rapid oscillations are attenuated.

prompt_blocks.text: Which endpoint statement matches $|H(j\omega)|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\omega RC)^2}}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: At $\omega=0$, the denominator is $1$, so the gain is $1$. As $\omega$ grows, the term $(\omega RC)^2$ dominates, so the magnitude tends to $0$, which is the low-pass pattern.

entries.lesson_core_move: Model the RC high-pass circuit by identifying the series capacitor, resistor-to-ground, and resistor-voltage output as the physical LTI filter used for later differential-equation and frequency-response analysis.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Series Capacitor and Resistor-to-Ground

image_slots.image_description: Clean black-and-white RC high-pass circuit schematic with an input source on the left labeled $v_{in}(t)$, a capacitor in series on the input path, a resistor from the output node to ground, and clear node labels showing the signal path from $v_{in}(t)$ to the output node. Emphasize the capacitor in series and the grounded resistor as the defining topology.

Clean black-and-white RC high-pass circuit schematic with the same capacitor-in-series and resistor-to-ground topology, but mirrored left-to-right with the labels changed so the learner must track the wiring rather than memorize positions. Keep the output node clear and emphasize the same high-pass topology.

prompt_blocks.text: In the RC high-pass circuit shown, which statement correctly identifies the series capacitor and the resistor-to-ground?

choice_blocks.text: The capacitor is in series with the input, and the resistor goes from the output node to ground.
The resistor is in series with the input, and the capacitor goes from the output node to ground.
The capacitor is in series with the input, and the resistor goes from the source node directly to ground.
The capacitor is in series with the input, and the resistor is connected across the capacitor instead of to ground.
The capacitor and resistor both sit in the series path from the input to the output node.

questions.correct_answer: The capacitor is in series with the input, and the resistor goes from the output node to ground.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Trace the path from $v_{in}(t)$ to the first passive element. That first element is the capacitor in series. Then follow the branch from the output node down to ground. That branch is the resistor-to-ground path.

prompt_blocks.text: In the mirrored RC high-pass schematic shown, which statement still correctly identifies the series capacitor and the resistor-to-ground?

choice_blocks.text: The capacitor is still the series element, and the resistor is still the branch that returns the output node to ground.
The resistor is still the series element, and the capacitor is still the branch that returns the output node to ground.
The capacitor is still in series, and the resistor is connected directly from the source node to ground.
The capacitor is still in series, and the resistor is connected across the capacitor instead of to ground.
The capacitor and resistor both sit in the same shunt branch to ground.

questions.correct_answer: The capacitor is still the series element, and the resistor is still the branch that returns the output node to ground.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The mirror change only affects the layout, not the topology. The first passive element on the input path is still the capacitor, and the branch from the output node to ground is still the resistor.

sections.section_title: Locating the Input Voltage and Resistor-Voltage Output

image_slots.image_description: High-pass RC schematic with the source on the left, a series capacitor, an output node, and a resistor to ground. Show an arrow labeled $v_{in}(t)$ at the source-side node before the capacitor. Show an arrow labeled $v_{out}(t)$ across the resistor from the output node down to ground. Make the output clearly across the resistor, not across the capacitor.

High-pass RC schematic with the source-side input marked $v_{in}(t)$, a series capacitor, and a resistor to ground at the output node. Emphasize the voltage across the resistor as $v_{out}(t)$ and keep the capacitor voltage unlabeled so the output port is unambiguous.

prompt_blocks.text: In the RC high-pass schematic, which labeling is correct for the input and output signals?

choice_blocks.text: $v_{in}(t)$ is at the source-side node, and $v_{out}(t)$ is across the resistor to ground.
$v_{in}(t)$ is across the resistor, and $v_{out}(t)$ is across the capacitor.
$v_{out}(t)$ is at the source-side node, and $v_{in}(t)$ is across the resistor.
$v_{in}(t)$ is at the source-side node, and $v_{out}(t)$ is at the ground node.
$v_{in}(t)$ is at the node after the capacitor, and $v_{out}(t)$ is across the resistor.

questions.correct_answer: $v_{in}(t)$ is at the source-side node, and $v_{out}(t)$ is across the resistor to ground.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The input is applied at the source-side node before the capacitor. The output is the resistor voltage, so it is measured across the resistor from the output node down to ground.

prompt_blocks.text: Where is $v_{out}(t)$ measured in the RC high-pass circuit?

choice_blocks.text: Across the resistor from the output node to ground.
Across the capacitor from the source-side node to the output node.
At the source-side node before the capacitor.
Across the entire series path from the source to ground.

questions.correct_answer: Across the resistor from the output node to ground.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: In this model, $v_{out}(t)$ is the voltage across the resistor, not across the capacitor and not at ground alone. That is the output port you carry into the rest of the RC high-pass analysis.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the High-Pass Circuit as an LTI System

image_slots.image_description: Clean RC high-pass schematic with the source-side input arrow labeled $v_{in}(t)$, the resistor-voltage output arrow labeled $v_{out}(t)$ across the resistor, the series capacitor, the resistor to ground, and a small annotation that it is a one-input, one-output LTI system with fixed passive elements.

Clean RC high-pass schematic with the output arrow across the resistor emphasized, the source-side input arrow labeled $v_{in}(t)$, the series capacitor, the resistor to ground, and a note that the capacitor and resistor are fixed passive elements in a one-input, one-output system.

prompt_blocks.text: Refer to the circuit diagram. Which statement correctly interprets the RC high-pass circuit as a one-input, one-output LTI system?

choice_blocks.text: The source-side signal is $v_{in}(t)$, the resistor voltage is $v_{out}(t)$, and the capacitor and resistor are fixed passive elements, so the circuit is a one-input, one-output LTI system.
The source-side signal is $v_{out}(t)$ and the resistor voltage is $v_{in}(t)$, so the input and output roles are reversed.
The output is across the capacitor, so the circuit is the low-pass model instead of the high-pass model.
The capacitor and resistor change with time, so the circuit is time-varying.
The circuit is nonlinear because the passive elements depend on the signal.

questions.correct_answer: The source-side signal is $v_{in}(t)$, the resistor voltage is $v_{out}(t)$, and the capacitor and resistor are fixed passive elements, so the circuit is a one-input, one-output LTI system.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The port labels identify the input and output: $v_{in}(t)$ enters at the source side and $v_{out}(t)$ is taken across the resistor. Because the capacitor and resistor are fixed passive elements, the circuit is a one-input, one-output LTI model.

prompt_blocks.text: Refer to the same diagram. Which statement correctly names the output node and the fixed passive elements in the high-pass model?

choice_blocks.text: The output is across the capacitor, and the capacitor and resistor change with time.
$v_{in}(t)$ is the output and $v_{out}(t)$ is the input, so the signal roles are reversed.
$v_{out}(t)$ is across the resistor, and the capacitor and resistor are fixed passive elements that define the LTI model.
The capacitor and resistor change with time, so the circuit is time-varying.
The circuit has no fixed input-output interpretation because only the source matters.

questions.correct_answer: $v_{out}(t)$ is across the resistor, and the capacitor and resistor are fixed passive elements that define the LTI model.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The output node is across the resistor, not the capacitor, and both passive elements are fixed. That is why the circuit is interpreted as a one-input, one-output LTI filter model.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing the High-Pass Model from the Low-Pass Model

image_slots.image_description: Side-by-side textbook-style circuit comparison showing the RC high-pass arrangement on the left and the RC low-pass arrangement on the right with the same orientation and line weight. In the high-pass diagram, show the capacitor in series with the input path, the resistor to ground, the input labeled $v_{in}(t)$, and the output labeled $v_{out}(t)$ across the resistor. In the low-pass diagram, show the resistor in series with the input path, the capacitor to ground, and the output across the capacitor. Keep both diagrams minimal so the topology difference is the main signal.

questions.correct_answer: A. The high-pass circuit with the capacitor in series, the resistor to ground, and the output across the resistor.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The high-pass model keeps the capacitor in series, the resistor to ground, and the output across the resistor.
Choice B is the low-pass arrangement, choice C moves the output to the capacitor, choice D mirrors the low-pass layout, and choice E swaps the input and output labels.

Focus on the output node and the placement of the passive elements.

questions.correct_answer: C. The high-pass circuit with the capacitor in series, the resistor to ground, and the output across the resistor.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The high-pass arrangement is the one with the capacitor first, the resistor to ground, and the output across the resistor.
Choices A and B are low-pass layouts, choice D moves the output to the capacitor, and choice E swaps the input and output labels.

entries.lesson_core_move: Derive the high-pass input-output differential equation from the RC circuit model by relating capacitor current, resistor current, input voltage, and output voltage.

sections.section_title: Writing the Input Voltage as Capacitor Voltage Plus Output Voltage

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=v_C(t)+y(t)$, which expression correctly isolates $v_C(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Subtract $y(t)$ from both sides of $x(t)=v_C(t)+y(t)$ to isolate the capacitor voltage. The result is $v_C(t)=x(t)-y(t)$, so choice A is correct.

prompt_blocks.text: If $v_{in}(t)=v_C(t)+v_{out}(t)$, which expression correctly isolates $v_C(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Subtract $v_{out}(t)$ from both sides of $v_{in}(t)=v_C(t)+v_{out}(t)$. That isolates $v_C(t)$ as $v_{in}(t)-v_{out}(t)$, so choice A is correct.

sections.section_title: Relating the Series Capacitor Current and Resistor Current

prompt_blocks.text: Which equation correctly states the shared branch current in the high-pass RC series branch?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The capacitor and resistor are in series, so they carry the same branch current. That shared-current relation is written before any voltage substitution happens.

prompt_blocks.text: If the capacitor current is $C\,\frac{dv_C(t)}{dt}$ and the resistor current is $\frac{y(t)}{R}$, which equation sets them equal?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: In a series branch, the same current flows through both elements, so the capacitor law and the resistor law are set equal directly. The resistor current uses the output voltage $y(t)$, not the input voltage $x(t)$.

sections.section_title: Substituting Output Voltage into the Capacitor Current Law

prompt_blocks.text: After substituting $v_C(t)=x(t)-y(t)$ into $i_C(t)=C\,\frac{dv_C(t)}{dt}$, which expression is equivalent?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $v_C(t)=x(t)-y(t)$ directly into the capacitor current law first, and keep the subtraction intact. The factor $C$ stays outside, so the equivalent expression is $i_C(t)=C\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x(t)-y(t)\bigr)$.

prompt_blocks.text: After expanding the derivative in $i_C(t)=C\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x(t)-y(t)\bigr)$, which expression is equivalent?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Differentiate the difference term by term, so the minus sign stays between the two derivatives. Keep the factor $C$ outside, giving $i_C(t)=C\,\bigl(x'(t)-y'(t)\bigr)$.

sections.section_title: Rearranging into the High-Pass Input-Output Differential Equation

prompt_blocks.text: Which differential equation is equivalent to $C\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x(t)-y(t)\bigr)=\frac{y(t)}{R}$ after rearranging?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply through by $R$ to get $RC\,\bigl(x'(t)-y'(t)\bigr)=y(t)$. Then move the $-RC\,y'(t)$ term to the left, which gives the standard form $RC\,\frac{dy(t)}{dt}+y(t)=RC\,\frac{dx(t)}{dt}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which differential equation is equivalent to $C\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(u(t)-v(t)\bigr)=\frac{v(t)}{R}$ after rearranging?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This is the same rearrangement with renamed variables. Clear the denominator, then move the output-derivative term to the left and the input-derivative term to the right to get $RC\,\frac{dv(t)}{dt}+v(t)=RC\,\frac{du(t)}{dt}$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert the high-pass differential equation into the frequency response \(H(j\omega)\) that maps sinusoidal input frequency to output amplitude scaling and phase shift.

sections.section_title: Replacing Derivatives with \(j\omega\) in the High-Pass Equation

prompt_blocks.text: Which equation results after replacing each derivative with $j\omega$ in $2RC\,\frac{dx(t)}{dt}=y(t)+3RC\,\frac{dy(t)}{dt}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Replace both derivatives with multiplication by $j\omega$ and keep the input-output variables the same.
The left derivative picks up the factor $2j\omega RC$, the right derivative picks up $3j\omega RC$, and the non-derivative term stays $Y(j\omega)$. So choice A is correct.

prompt_blocks.text: Which equation results after replacing each derivative with $j\omega$ in $RC\,\frac{dx(t)}{dt}-RC\,\frac{dy(t)}{dt}=y(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply the derivative rule to both terms and keep the minus sign already present in the equation.
The left side keeps both derivative terms with their $j\omega RC$ factors, and the right side stays $Y(j\omega)$. So choice A is correct.

sections.section_title: Solving the High-Pass Equation for \(H(j\omega)\)

prompt_blocks.text: Starting from $j\omega RC\,X(j\omega)=(1+j\omega RC)Y(j\omega)$, which expression is $H(j\omega)=\frac{Y(j\omega)}{X(j\omega)}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Isolate the output-to-input ratio $Y(j\omega)/X(j\omega)$ and name it $H(j\omega)$. That gives $H(j\omega)=\frac{j\omega RC}{1+j\omega RC}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Starting from $2j\omega RC\,X(j\omega)=(1+2j\omega RC)Y(j\omega)$, which expression is $H(j\omega)=\frac{Y(j\omega)}{X(j\omega)}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The same isolation step applies, with the factor 2 carried through both sides. Solving for $Y(j\omega)/X(j\omega)$ gives $H(j\omega)=\frac{2j\omega RC}{1+2j\omega RC}$.

sections.section_title: Using \(H(j\omega)\) to Write the High-Pass Sinusoidal Output

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t)=4\cos(\omega t-\pi/3)$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{j\omega RC}{1+j\omega RC}$, which output matches the high-pass response in amplitude-phase form?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The output keeps the same frequency. Multiply the amplitude by $|H(j\omega)|=\frac{\omega RC}{\sqrt{1+(\omega RC)^2}}$ and add the phase $\angle H(j\omega)=\frac{\pi}{2}-\tan^{-1}(\omega RC)$ to the input phase.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=2\cos(\omega t+\pi/6)$ and $\omega RC=1$, which output is correct in amplitude-phase form?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: When $\omega RC=1$, the gain is $|H(j\omega)|=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and the phase shift is $\angle H(j\omega)=\frac{\pi}{4}$. So the output amplitude is $\frac{2}{\sqrt2}$ and the output phase is the input phase plus $\frac{\pi}{4}$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the RC high-pass magnitude response from its frequency response and interpret how it attenuates low frequencies while passing high frequencies.

sections.section_title: Computing \(|H(j\omega)|\) from the High-Pass Frequency Response

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression is equal to $|H(j\omega)|$ for $H(j\omega)=\frac{j\omega RC}{1+j\omega RC}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Take magnitudes term by term. $|j\omega RC|=\omega RC$ and $|1+j\omega RC|=\sqrt{1+(\omega RC)^2}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression is equal to $|G(j\omega)|$ for $G(j\omega)=\frac{j\omega(2RC)}{1+j\omega(2RC)}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same magnitude rule as before, but replace $RC$ with $2RC$. The numerator magnitude is $2\omega RC$ and the denominator magnitude is $\sqrt{1+(2\omega RC)^2}$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Low-Frequency Attenuation

prompt_blocks.text: For $\omega RC \ll 1$, which expression best approximates $|H(j\omega)|$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: When $\omega RC \ll 1$, the denominator satisfies $\sqrt{1+(\omega RC)^2}\approx 1$. So $|H(j\omega)|\approx \omega RC$, which is small and proportional to frequency.

prompt_blocks.text: If $\omega RC = 0.02$, which value best approximates $|H(j\omega)|$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because $0.02 \ll 1$, the low-frequency approximation gives $|H(j\omega)|\approx \omega RC$. Substituting $\omega RC = 0.02$ gives $|H(j\omega)|\approx 0.02$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting High-Frequency Passage

prompt_blocks.text: For $\omega RC \gg 1$, which expression best approximates $|H(j\omega)|$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: When $\omega RC$ is very large, the $(\omega RC)^2$ term dominates inside the square root, so the denominator is approximately $\omega RC$.
So the high-frequency gain is near $1$, not $0$ and not a term that grows or shrinks with $\omega RC$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}|H(j\omega)|$ for the RC high-pass filter?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The same asymptotic comparison applies here: numerator and denominator grow at the same rate, so the ratio approaches $1$.
That limit is the meaning of high-frequency passage: very high frequencies come through with near-unity gain.

sections.section_title: Reading the High-Pass Magnitude Response as a Filter

prompt_blocks.text: Using $|H(j\omega)|=\frac{\omega RC}{\sqrt{1+(\omega RC)^2}}$, which statement best describes the RC circuit as frequency increases?

choice_blocks.text: It attenuates low frequencies and passes high frequencies.
It passes low frequencies and attenuates high frequencies.
Its gain stays flat at the same value for all frequencies.

questions.correct_answer: It attenuates low frequencies and passes high frequencies.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The magnitude response goes to $0$ as $\omega\to0$ and to $1$ as $\omega\to\infty$. That means low-frequency components are strongly attenuated, while high-frequency components pass with near-unity gain. So the circuit is a high-pass filter.

prompt_blocks.text: If $|H(j\omega)|\to0$ as $\omega\to0$ and $|H(j\omega)|\to1$ as $\omega\to\infty$, which description fits the RC circuit best?

choice_blocks.text: High-pass filter: it suppresses low frequencies and passes high frequencies.
Low-pass filter: it passes low frequencies and suppresses high frequencies.
Band-pass filter: only middle frequencies pass through.
All-pass filter: the gain stays the same for every frequency.

questions.correct_answer: High-pass filter: it suppresses low frequencies and passes high frequencies.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Those endpoint limits say the gain is near $0$ at low frequency and near $1$ at high frequency. That is exactly the behavior of a high-pass filter, because it suppresses low-frequency input while passing high-frequency input.

entries.lesson_title: Comparing RC Low-Pass and High-Pass Filters
entries.lesson_core_move: Distinguish RC low-pass and high-pass filters by comparing their magnitude-response trends to predict which frequency components are passed or attenuated.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing RC Low-Pass and High-Pass Filters
sections.section_title: Comparing Low-Frequency Behavior

prompt_blocks.text: A sinusoid with $\omega \ll 1/RC$ is applied to both an RC low-pass filter and an RC high-pass filter. Which filter passes it more strongly?

choice_blocks.text: Both filters pass it equally strongly.
Neither filter passes it well because the signal is at the cutoff frequency.
The RC low-pass filter attenuates it more strongly.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is $\omega \ll 1/RC$, so this is the low-frequency endpoint. Compare the endpoint magnitudes, not the circuit equations.
So the RC low-pass filter passes the sinusoid more strongly, and the RC high-pass filter attenuates it.

prompt_blocks.text: At $\omega \ll 1/RC$, which comparison is correct for the RC filter magnitudes?

choice_blocks.text: Both magnitudes are equal and near 1.
Both magnitudes are about the same because $\omega \ll 1/RC$ puts the signal at the cutoff region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: At the low-frequency endpoint, the low-pass response is near its maximum while the high-pass response is near zero.
That is why the low-pass output is larger and the high-pass output is smaller for the same low-frequency input.

Both magnitudes are about the same because $\omega \gg 1/RC$ puts the signal at the cutoff region.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing RC Low-Pass and High-Pass Filters
sections.section_title: Predicting Passed and Attenuated Frequency Components

prompt_blocks.text: A signal has components at $250$ Hz and $8$ kHz. Which statement correctly describes an RC low-pass filter and an RC high-pass filter?

choice_blocks.text: The RC low-pass filter passes $250$ Hz and attenuates $8$ kHz; the RC high-pass filter attenuates $250$ Hz and passes $8$ kHz.
The RC low-pass filter attenuates $250$ Hz and passes $8$ kHz; the RC high-pass filter attenuates $250$ Hz and passes $8$ kHz.
The RC low-pass filter passes $250$ Hz and attenuates $8$ kHz; the RC high-pass filter passes $250$ Hz and attenuates $8$ kHz.
Both filters pass the component closer to the cutoff frequency and attenuate the other component.

questions.correct_answer: The RC low-pass filter passes $250$ Hz and attenuates $8$ kHz; the RC high-pass filter attenuates $250$ Hz and passes $8$ kHz.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The lower frequency is the one a low-pass filter passes, and the higher frequency is the one a high-pass filter passes. Here, $250$ Hz is the low component and $8$ kHz is the high component, so the pass and attenuate labels reverse between the two filter types.

prompt_blocks.text: A signal has components at $60$ Hz and $6$ kHz. Which statement correctly describes an RC high-pass filter?

choice_blocks.text: The RC high-pass filter passes $6$ kHz and attenuates $60$ Hz.
The RC high-pass filter passes $60$ Hz and attenuates $6$ kHz.
The RC high-pass filter passes both components.
The RC high-pass filter attenuates both components.
The RC high-pass filter passes the component closer to the cutoff frequency and attenuates the other component.

questions.correct_answer: The RC high-pass filter passes $6$ kHz and attenuates $60$ Hz.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: An RC high-pass filter does the opposite of an RC low-pass filter: it passes the higher-frequency component and attenuates the lower-frequency component. Here, $6$ kHz is passed and $60$ Hz is attenuated.

entries.lesson_core_move: Predict how changing \(RC\) shifts the cutoff behavior and magnitude-response transition of RC low-pass and high-pass filters.

sections.section_title: Identifying $RC$ as the Cutoff-Setting Quantity

prompt_blocks.text: Two RC low-pass filters have $(R,C)=(500\,\Omega,2\,\mu\text{F})$ and $(R,C)=(1\,\text{k}\Omega,1\,\mu\text{F})$. Which statement is correct?

choice_blocks.text: They have the same cutoff frequency.
The first filter has the lower cutoff because its resistance is smaller.
The second filter has the lower cutoff because its capacitance is smaller.
The first filter has the higher cutoff because larger $RC$ gives higher cutoff.
The cutoff cannot be determined from $RC$ alone.

questions.correct_answer: They have the same cutoff frequency.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Compute the products: $500\,\Omega \cdot 2\,\mu\text{F}=10^{-3}\,\text{s}$ and $1\,\text{k}\Omega \cdot 1\,\mu\text{F}=10^{-3}\,\text{s}$. Since $\omega_c=1/RC$, equal $RC$ means equal cutoff frequency.

prompt_blocks.text: Two RC low-pass filters have $(R,C)=(2\,\text{k}\Omega,2\,\mu\text{F})$ and $(R,C)=(1\,\text{k}\Omega,1\,\mu\text{F})$. Which filter has the lower cutoff frequency?

choice_blocks.text: The second filter, because its resistance is smaller.
The second filter, because its capacitance is smaller.
The second filter, because larger $RC$ gives higher cutoff.
They have the same cutoff frequency.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Compute the products: $2\,\text{k}\Omega \cdot 2\,\mu\text{F}=4\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}$ and $1\,\text{k}\Omega \cdot 1\,\mu\text{F}=10^{-3}\,\text{s}$. Since $\omega_c=1/RC$, the larger $RC$ gives the lower cutoff, so the first filter has the lower cutoff frequency.

sections.section_title: Predicting a Low-Pass Magnitude Response After Changing $RC$

prompt_blocks.text: A low-pass filter has cutoff $\omega_c = 1/RC$. If $RC$ doubles, what happens to the cutoff and the magnitude-response transition?

choice_blocks.text: The cutoff halves, and the transition shifts left.
The cutoff doubles, and the transition shifts left.
The cutoff halves, and the transition shifts right.
The cutoff stays the same because only the filter type matters.
The cutoff doubles, and the transition shifts right.

questions.correct_answer: The cutoff halves, and the transition shifts left.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because $\omega_c = 1/RC$, doubling $RC$ cuts $\omega_c$ in half. For a low-pass filter, a smaller cutoff moves the transition to lower frequency, so the bend shifts left.

prompt_blocks.text: A low-pass filter has cutoff $\omega_c = 1/RC$. If $RC$ is halved, what happens to the cutoff and the magnitude-response transition?

choice_blocks.text: The cutoff doubles, and the transition shifts right.
The cutoff halves, and the transition shifts right.
The cutoff doubles, and the transition shifts left.
The cutoff stays the same because only $R$ changes but $C$ does not.
The cutoff halves, and the transition shifts left.

questions.correct_answer: The cutoff doubles, and the transition shifts right.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Halving $RC$ makes $1/RC$ twice as large, so the cutoff doubles. For a low-pass filter, a larger cutoff moves the transition to higher frequency, so the bend shifts right.

sections.section_title: Predicting a High-Pass Magnitude Response After Changing $RC$

prompt_blocks.text: A high-pass filter has cutoff $\omega_c = 1/RC$. If $RC$ doubles, what happens to the cutoff frequency, and where does a frequency just below the original cutoff move relative to the passband?

choice_blocks.text: The cutoff doubles, and the frequency is farther from the passband.
The cutoff halves, and the frequency is closer to the passband.
The cutoff halves, and the frequency is farther from the passband.
The cutoff stays the same, and the frequency is closer to the passband.
The cutoff doubles, and the frequency is closer to the passband.

questions.correct_answer: The cutoff halves, and the frequency is closer to the passband.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cutoff still follows $\omega_c = 1/RC$. Doubling $RC$ lowers the cutoff, so the transition moves to a lower frequency.
A frequency just below the original cutoff is now above the new cutoff, so it is closer to the passband and less attenuated than before.

prompt_blocks.text: A high-pass filter has cutoff $\omega_c = 1/RC$. If $RC$ is cut in half, what happens to the cutoff frequency, and where does a frequency just above the original cutoff move relative to the passband?

choice_blocks.text: The cutoff halves, and the frequency is farther from the passband.
The cutoff doubles, and the frequency is farther from the passband.
The cutoff doubles, and the frequency is closer to the passband.
The cutoff stays the same, and the frequency is farther from the passband.
The cutoff halves, and the frequency is closer to the passband.

questions.correct_answer: The cutoff doubles, and the frequency is farther from the passband.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The same cutoff rule applies: $\omega_c = 1/RC$. Halving $RC$ raises the cutoff, so the transition moves to a higher frequency.
A frequency just above the original cutoff can now fall below the new cutoff, so it is farther from the passband and more attenuated than before.

sections.section_title: Comparing Magnitude-Response Transitions for Different $RC$ Values

prompt_blocks.text: Two RC filters satisfy $RC_1 < RC_2$. Which statement is correct about the cutoff frequencies and magnitude-response transitions of both the low-pass and high-pass responses?

choice_blocks.text: The filter with $RC_2$ has the lower cutoff frequency, and both its low-pass and high-pass transitions shift to lower frequency.
The filter with $RC_1$ has the lower cutoff frequency, and both its low-pass and high-pass transitions shift to lower frequency.
The filter with $RC_2$ has the lower cutoff frequency, but only the low-pass transition shifts to lower frequency.
The filter with $RC_2$ has the lower cutoff frequency, but only the high-pass transition shifts to lower frequency.
The filter with $RC_2$ has the higher cutoff frequency, and both transitions shift to higher frequency.

questions.correct_answer: The filter with $RC_2$ has the lower cutoff frequency, and both its low-pass and high-pass transitions shift to lower frequency.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because cutoff frequency is inversely proportional to $RC$, the larger product $RC_2$ gives the lower cutoff. That same ordering applies to both the low-pass and high-pass magnitude-response transitions, so both move to lower frequency together.

prompt_blocks.text: Two RC filters satisfy $RC_A = 3RC_B$. Which statement correctly compares the cutoff frequencies and transition locations for both filter types?

choice_blocks.text: The filter with $RC_B$ has the lower cutoff frequency, and both its low-pass and high-pass transitions shift to lower frequency.
The filter with $RC_A$ has the lower cutoff frequency, and both its low-pass and high-pass transitions shift to lower frequency.
The filter with $RC_A$ has the lower cutoff frequency, but only the low-pass transition shifts to lower frequency.
The filter with $RC_A$ has the lower cutoff frequency, but only the high-pass transition shifts to lower frequency.
The filter with $RC_A$ has the higher cutoff frequency, and both transitions shift to higher frequency.

questions.correct_answer: The filter with $RC_A$ has the lower cutoff frequency, and both its low-pass and high-pass transitions shift to lower frequency.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Since $RC_A$ is larger than $RC_B$, it has the smaller cutoff frequency. The low-pass and high-pass transitions follow the same cutoff ordering, so both shift left for the $RC_A$ filter.
